There are often issues with mods on large subs, but we have managed to avoid or quell any problems. So I thought I might explain how. I sometime see mod abuse, and it is great when the community rails against it. But other times it is just miscommunication or a misunderstanding, and I think those can generally be avoided.

So here are some pointers :

1 - Be transparent in everything you do.

2 - It is not your sub. It belongs to the users. If you can not understand that, you will have problems.

3 - Never impose arbitrary rules. Ask for input before adding rules, and don't add them if they are unpopular.

4 - Keep rules as simple and clear as you can. Do not leave them so vague that people are unsure of what breaks them. But also do not write up a legal code, that has sub-sections and paragraphs. Nobody will read them if you do.

5 - Always hear out complaints fully. You do not have to do whatever you are told. But you do need to listen, and let them explain themselves.

6 - Respond to all feedback, even if you are not going to do anything about it. Respond so they know they were heard, and tell them what you think. Politely.

7 - Spend time in the new queue. Sometimes we do not have enough knights of new. If a post does not get at least one upvoat I don't think it will appear in /v/all. So unless you have a large sub (and sometimes even then) you might need to hang out in the new queue in order to jump start the good posts.

8 - Before removing a post or comment, reply to it and state why it is being removed.

9 - Warn first time offenders and do not remove their first violation unless it is an extreme case.

10 - An engaged community is your most important asset. They will flag the spam, they will add more content and discussion, and if someone becomes angry with you, they will defend you better than you can.

11 - Do not get angry when someone attacks you or acts like an asshole. It is going to happen, keep your cool. Respond in a calm and rational way, and stop responding once you've made yourself clear. Do not get pulled into a meaningless flame war. Take the high road.

12 - If you find a post that broke a rule, but discussion has already begun, or it has received a number of upvoats, do not remove it. If it sparked conversation or interest, then it should be left. Take the opportunity to remind everyone of the rule and that it would have been removed if caught earlier, but let the users deal with it at that point.

13 - Be transparent in everything you do.

Rule 1 is difficult though.

Be Civilized: This means no racism, sexism, homophobia, transphobia, bigotry, assholery or otherwise disrespectful commentary.

I understand the intent, but it is too open ended.
The difference between a disrespectful comment and a genuine opinion can be very subjective. A mod should not have to use their opinion. That is a difficult one to create an objective rule for. My advice would be to make it a 'guideline' and rather than delete the comments just hand out reminders of the guideline and count on the community to downvoat them. You can add flair for posts that break it. And comments like "Hurr durr you're a trans fag" could be removed as spam.

Also I would suggest making the post about rule feedback easier to find. Add a link in the sidebar or sticky it.

Unfortunately for you, your topic is one that can be controversial around here, and you will probably be targeted by people with an agenda. My best advice on that is, do not let them get to you, do not act rashly, and it is always better to remove too little, than too much.

You, even more than other mods, will need help from your community. Engage them, and support them, and pray that they help you out when you come under unfair attack.
